title: SPICE-Q and Large-Scale Quantum Chip Production
authors: Cai, Ling Qiao, Bin Yang, Fumin Luo, Chang Liu, WeiGui Guo, GuoRong Zhang, XueFei Liu, Qinglang Guo, Bin Wu
abstract: We propose SPICE-Q, a SPICE-inspired design-technology co-optimization framework for superconducting quantum processors. Rather than replacing tools such as HFSS, Qiskit Metal, pyEPR, SQcircuit, SQuADDS, scqubits, or QuTiP, SPICE-Q aims to connect them through a unified, traceable data chain spanning process rules, layout, electromagnetic simulation, energy-participation-ratio and circuit quantization, Hamiltonian extraction, noise analysis, cryogenic test, and manufacturing feedback. The central mapping is from process and PDK constraints to layout geometry, electromagnetic modes, equivalent circuit parameters, effective Hamiltonians, and finally metrics such as frequency, coupling, anharmonicity, decoherence, readout performance, and yield. This flow must capture Josephson-junction variability, transmon frequency allocation, resonator and Purcell constraints, coupler crosstalk, microwave routing, 3D interconnects, material/interface loss, package modes, and wafer-scale process statistics. By introducing standardized model interfaces, statistical parameter models, model cards, version governance, and closed-loop calibration from cryogenic and fabrication data, SPICE-Q frames superconducting quantum-chip design as an engineering workflow rather than a collection of isolated simulations. We argue that scalable and fault-tolerant quantum processors will require such a continuous model chain from device physics and electromagnetic fields to quantum dynamics, noise, manufacturability, and system-level yield.
summary: This paper introduces SPICE-Q, a comprehensive framework designed to industrialize superconducting quantum chip design. It solves the problem of fragmented simulation tools by creating a unified data chain connecting electromagnetics, device physics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and manufacturing statistics. This shift treats quantum hardware development as a rigorous engineering workflow necessary for scaling fault-tolerant computation.
main_problem: The design of large-scale, fault-tolerant superconducting quantum processors requires a unified engineering workflow that connects device physics to system performance.
main_result: SPICE-Q proposes a Design-Technology Co-Optimization (DTCO) framework that treats quantum chip design as an industrial engineering process rather than isolated simulations.
method: The framework unifies disparate simulation tools (EM solvers, Hamiltonian dynamics, classical circuit simulators) through standardized model interfaces and a traceable data chain.
model_or_system: The system is superconducting quantum chips built from Josephson junctions, modeled by coupling electromagnetic field solutions to effective Hamiltonians describing qubit dynamics and noise channels.
key_observables: Frequency, coupling strength, anharmonicity, decoherence times ($T_1/T_2$), readout performance, and overall manufacturing yield.
important_parameters: Process constraints (PDK), Josephson junction variability ($\delta I_c$), resonator quality factors ($Q$), and 3D interconnect parasitics.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that scaling requires treating the entire design process—from physics to fabrication statistics—as a single, continuous, model-driven engineering workflow.
paper_structure: The paper builds an analogy with classical SPICE development (moving from physical equations to parameterized models) and applies this structure to quantum computing, detailing the necessary integration points between EM simulation, Hamiltonian extraction, and statistical yield analysis.
why_interesting: It provides a crucial engineering roadmap for applying advanced open-system dynamics and many-body techniques by formalizing the interface between electromagnetic field theory and quantum information processing models.
